sections.html: The Indian glass fish, Chanda ranga, is a small ambassid from South and Southeast Asia, with translucent skin that shows its bones and organs. For many years it was injected with luminous dyes on Asian fish farms and sold as 'painted' glass fish, and most injected fish do not survive more than a few months. It is found most often in freshwater, frequently soft and acidic, and needs no added salt. Parambassis lala and C. siamensis are often imported under its name.
India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia and Cambodia. Introduced to Japan and Hong Kong.
It usually inhabits areas of slow moving or still water.
An aquarium with dimensions of 80 × 30 × 30 cm (31 × 12 × 12 in) or equivalent (about 72 litres) should be the smallest considered.

A dark substrate will help to make this shy species less nervous and encourage it to display its best colours. Provide cover by planting some areas of the tank densely, along with some floating vegetation. Rocks and driftwood can also be used. The fish can live in both freshwater and slightly brackish conditions.
Relatively unfussy and will accept most live, frozen and dried foods.

C. ranga is peaceful and shy and should not be combined with vigorous or aggressive species. The choice of tankmates is also governed by the type of water in which it is being kept. In freshwater conditions, it can be kept with barbs, livebearers, smaller rainbowfish, loaches and many other small tropicals. In the brackish aquarium, mollies, bumblebee gobies and chromides are all possibilities. The Indian glass fish is a shoaling species and will not do well if kept singly or in pairs. Aim for a group of at least 6. Males do become somewhat territorial when spawning but physical damage is rare.

Males have blue edging to the dorsal and anal fins and are a slightly deeper yellow on the body than females. These differences are more apparent when the fish are breeding, as the colours become more intense. The swim bladder (which is clearly visible) has a pointed back edge in males.

Not too difficult, although the fry are difficult to raise. Provide the fish with a heavily planted aquarium of around 76 × 30 × 30 cm (30 × 12 × 12 in). Stock it with 6-8 adult fish. It is an advantage if the tank is situated so that it receives direct sunlight in the morning. Condition the group with a high quality, varied diet. During this period, maintain them at a temperature of around 21–24 °C (70–75 °F). A pH around neutral should be fine.

When the fish are in breeding condition (look for an intensifying of the colours of the males, and round bellies on the females), perform a large water change with warmer water (around 26.5–29 °C / 80–84 °F) in the evening. The fish should spawn the following morning. Each pair may deposit up to 200 eggs, and these will be found amongst the vegetation, stuck to plant leaves and stems. The adult fish can be removed at this point.

The eggs are very sensitive to fungus and the entire tank should be dosed with a weak solution of methylene blue, or similar, in order to prevent this. They will hatch in around 24 hours and will be seen hanging from the plants. They become free swimming in another 3-4 days. They are quite difficult to raise, as they do not actively seek food. Instead they wait for morsels to drift by. It is suggested to feed quite heavily with brine shrimp nauplii and create a slow current in the tank. Regular small water changes will be required in order to keep the water conditions perfect.

The common name of this species arose because its translucent skin means that the bone structure and internal organs are clearly visible. For many years it has been artificially injected with luminous dyes on fish farms in Asia and then sold as "Painted" glass fish or "Disco fish". This act involves injecting the fish repeatedly with a large needle and most fish do not survive more than a few months afterwards. Whilst painted fish of this and other species are still available in many countries, protracted campaigning has seen them virtually removed from UK stores.

Most resources state that this species requires the addition of salt to its water, often stating that it is susceptible to fungal infections when kept in freshwater. This is not true. Whilst the fish can be acclimatised to mildly brackish water (and are found in brackish conditions in some of their habitats in nature), it is found most often in freshwater. Additionally, many of these freshwater habitats actually contain quite soft, acidic water. When purchasing this fish, ask your dealer what conditions they are being kept in. If they are in freshwater, there is no need to add salt to the tank.

The brackish myth, the susceptibility of the painted fish to disease and the fact that this is quite a short-lived species may have given rise to the belief that this fish is hard to keep. In reality, it is a pretty and peaceful species, well-suited to many community tanks. Several closely related species are often imported as C. ranga, as they look very similar. The most common are Parambassis lala and C. siamensis. Lala can be distinguished by its small (about 4 cm) adult size and the presence of three vertical bars behind the eye. Ranga has a dark area behind the eye, whilst siamensis has no patterning here. C. siamensis is also a more elongate fish than the other 2 species.
